text:
Chapter Fifteen


Arthur pushed Willoughby’s door closed until it latched. His heart hadn’t stopped pounding since he heard the sound in the alley, since Maggie had dug her nails into his arm. He had been so sure that something much worse than a wraith was stalking them, and every fear he’d had the moment Maggie told him she’d walked all the way from Hawthorn, since she’d insisted on helping with the pall, seemed to have come true in an instant. His thoughts were a rush—She was only out tonight because of me, only here so late because we had to go over every one of my mistakes—and if he didn’t get a grip, he was going to have a panic attack right here among the paperbacks.


Maggie was watching him, so he said around the lump in his throat, “I’m going to browse for a minute, if that’s okay?”


Her expression brightened, and, gods below, she was beautiful. “I was hoping you’d suggest that.” Her apple cheeks were pink with the excitement or the chill, he wasn’t sure which, and he remembered the way the flush had spread across her face as they’d danced surrounded by bonfires. He wanted to reach for her, but to his relief, she immediately disappeared up the rickety staircase beside the register, leaving him staring after her and worrying one of the buttons on his sweater.


Willoughby’s was two bright floors with books tucked into every possible corner. The new books were on the first floor, where glossy paperbacks with deckle edges and sleek hardcovers with dust jackets like butter lined tables and shelves. Upstairs were the used books and rare collections, which seemed to be where Maggie was heading. He breathed in the smell of dust, paper, and glue, a smell that always seemed a little bit like home, and tried to calm his racing heart.


If he was being honest with himself, it wasn’t just the wraith that had him unsettled. He owed Maggie the truth about what happened on Beltane, and the longer he went on without telling her, the guiltier he felt. He had opened his mouth more than once to tell her over the course of the afternoon, but he couldn’t do it. He was a coward, instead deciding on the spot that Rory’s plan, flawed as it was, was better than seeing her face fall in disappointment when he admitted he was the one who had kissed her. There was something fragile between them, something that drew them together like beads on a string, and he didn’t want to be the one who broke it. Even as he half feared he was imagining it.


If she could just remember on her own…but nothing he had tried so far had seemed to break the spell. Maybe she had already forgotten the night they’d shared. Maybe it had meant nothing to her at all. He’d thought, perhaps, buying her a coffee like he’d bought her a drink on the beach would ignite her memory, but nothing had happened as their fingers touched when he handed her the cup. As they’d entered Glinda’s, he’d barely had the nerve to reach out and let his hand graze her back where he’d held her as they danced, but all that had gotten him was a well-deserved glare over her shoulder. He thought he’d seen a glimmer of recognition in her expression as she’d sucked on the honeysuckle candy, but that, too, was in his head. He didn’t know what to do, but he knew they needed to get back to Hawthorn before the sun set.


Arthur grabbed a book off the table without looking at the cover and walked upstairs. He found Maggie right away, sitting in the seat of a large half-moon window that looked down on the street below. She had a book propped on her knees and a small stack on the plush quilted cushion beside her. Precarious shelves were crafted around the window and stuffed at all angles, creating an archway of books. He recognized a few of the spines as some of the more well-known Diadhan legends and epic poems that were the focus of Maggie’s research.


He wanted to sit down beside her. No, he wanted to gather her into his arms and drape her legs over his until she was curled around him. He wanted to forget the pall and the ghouls and the wraiths. Wanted both of them to get lost in whatever they were reading until the faefire glow of the streetlamps blinked on and the stars winked into view. He wanted something he couldn’t have.


When she saw him, she pushed her books out of the way and patted the cushion next to her. They should be walking back to Maggie’s apartment, but suddenly it seemed a lot less important than the chance that their legs might brush against each other like they had while they danced. They sat on opposite ends of the bench, leaning against the curve of the window, their legs bent. His seemed awkward and gangly, taking up far too much space, but she didn’t seem to mind. The window afforded them a view of Hawthorn. Ilex Hall rose out of the trees like a beacon with its arched walkways and russet brick. Beyond it, the edge of the Wilds loomed, alive and hungry.


He was staring out the window when Maggie said quietly, “The first year I moved to Galloway, I didn’t really know anyone. I came here a lot.” When he looked over at her, she was inspecting something on her knee. “I felt a little lost, I think. I was…” She paused, searching for the right words. “I was so burnt out after grad school, and I needed a new focus, but I had no idea what it would be. I didn’t trust myself anymore.”


Even though she wasn’t looking at him, he nodded. Every move he’d made over the past year—quitting his job at Dartwood, moving to Atlantia, taking the job at Hawthorn—was tinged with uncertainty. And now, the kiss on Beltane, the pall, his disastrous decision to share an office with Maggie…he was even less sure he’d done the right thing.


She gestured to the books around her. “I fell in love with Diadhan because my grandmother had a collection of translated Diadhan romances. Books and books of them that I’d read on summer vacation. Coming here felt a little bit like reminding myself what I loved about Diadhan in the first place. And, one afternoon, I was rereading Branagh’s Aubade. There’s a line in that poem—do you know it?” she asked eagerly, finally looking up at him. He smiled. He couldn’t help himself. He didn’t know why she was telling him this, but he wanted to do everything he could to keep her talking. He wanted to know everything about her.


“I read it once, a long time ago,” he said, though that wasn’t entirely true.


“Well, there’s a line in the fifteenth stanza that has been translated about a dozen different ways. I was reading the original and wondered if it was an idiom whose exact meaning had been mistranslated. I read Diadhan text after Diadhan text to try to find another use of it, and it was during one of those reading sessions that I had the idea for my research. You know that feeling, don’t you? That kind of what-if that leads to another what-if that leads to a why. So I have this bench and this window to thank.”


Arthur watched her look out the window. There was a wistful, sad expression on her face that he didn’t understand. “I used to come here, too.” She looked up at him in surprise. “The year after Simon was born, I’d fly out in the summer. To keep up with my research, I’d drive out to Galloway and work in the alchemy lab. It’s how I got to know Dean Clearwater and Dean Bobbin.”


“I didn’t know that.”


Arthur shrugged. “I kept to myself. And, on weekends, sometimes I’d bring Simon out here to get away from the city and give my brother a couple hours to run errands.”


How long had their lives been running in this parallel until they crashed together last August? It was strange to imagine another world where the Arthur he’d been four years ago ran into Maggie. He’d been a different man then. One more concerned with his own ambition, with making a name for himself, than anything else. Would they have given each other more than a passing glance? The silence stretched on between them, but it wasn’t awkward or unpleasant now. Eventually, Maggie’s lips, with their perfect divot, curved into a soft smile, and her attention returned to the view of the college and the Wilds beyond.


She reminded him so much of the Maggie he’d first seen on Beltane, sitting in the sand far from the party. And after he’d made that inexplicable decision to sit down next to her, he’d been sitting much like this, with his leg bent. All of it felt so familiar to him, but it seemed to do nothing to jog Maggie’s memory.


“Did you find something?” She gestured to the book in his hand, the one he’d forgotten all about as she talked. The one he hadn’t bothered to glance at before he’d picked it up.


He looked down: Difficult Conversations at Work: Talking to Colleagues with Ease. His ears grew hot and, he knew from experience, turned a blaring red that peeked out from beneath his hair. “Oh,” she said around a grin.


“It’s for my stepmom.”


“Sure,” she said as she gathered up her small stack of books in her arms. “We should get going. The sun is setting soon.”


He wasn’t sure if she said it because she was truly afraid of what they might encounter in the darkness, or if she was just giving him an easy out. Either way, he was grateful, and the gesture was enough to make his chest ache.



—


They’d just reached Maggie’s apartment building when the last of the sun finally sank beneath the horizon. Even if she hadn’t pointed out the apartment on the second floor, he would have known it was hers based on the balcony alone. A delicate crystal suncatcher hung from one corner and a wind chime in another. The balcony was covered with plants in colorful painted pots, but they all looked a little wilted in the gloom.


“Thank you for walking me home.” He was determined to wait and see Maggie walk through her apartment door, preferably with some indication that she had locked it behind her, but she didn’t say good night or walk up the stairs.


“It really wasn’t a big deal,” he said as Maggie reached into her tote bag and pulled out her keys. She clicked a button, and the headlights on a small purple coupe blinked on. “What are you—”


“Get in.” She was already opening the driver’s side door as she said, “I’ll drive you back to your car at Bean There.”


“You don’t need to do that.”


Maggie gave him a withering look over the hood of her car. “Dean Clearwater will reject my tenure application if a ghoul eats you on my watch. Then he’d murder me.”


“Huh.” Arthur crossed his arms, not even attempting to hide the smug look on his face. “I thought you said it was safe to walk?”


She rolled her eyes. “Yeah, two hours ago. In the daylight.” She gestured to the mist settling around them into a dense fog that collected at their ankles. A low rumbling came from the Wilds that sent an animal shiver down Arthur’s spine. It was followed by a crystalline screech that, thankfully, sounded like it was miles away.


“Is this what it sounds like every night?” He felt the familiar tug of his guilt.


“Since the pall.”


He shuddered. “How do you sleep?”


“Earplugs.” She glared at him with an expression that so clearly said, Well, what are you waiting for?


“Fine,” he finally said, walking to the passenger side of her car. “But you promise me you’ll drive right back here?”


“Oh, see, I thought you’d follow me back home in your car, and then I’d insist on following you to Atlantia, until you followed me back here and we got stuck in a never-ending courtesy loop that we traversed until we joined the wraiths in the Wilds, turning ourselves into the very thing we are afraid of.”


Arthur pushed up his glasses as he looked at her with raised eyebrows, but then he couldn’t help the laugh that escaped. The sound felt strange in his mouth, the lightness that came with it even stranger in his chest.


Maggie had a satisfied look on her face. Then she put her hand over her heart. “I’ll come straight home; I swear it. In fact, you couldn’t pay me to go back out tonight.”


Truthfully, Arthur didn’t exactly feel good about walking back through town in the dark, especially as another splintering banshee cry, this one decidedly closer, raised the hair on his arms.


He slid into the car, far too tiny for his tall frame, as Maggie started the engine. “I hope Dean Clearwater would be just as furious if I lost his best linguist.”


“Oh, well, that’s Dr. Habib, for sure.”


“Fine, his best—” But as he turned to click in his seat belt, his shoulder knocked something hanging from her rearview mirror. When he realized what it was, there weren’t any other coherent thoughts in his head. He froze.


“His best what?”


But Arthur didn’t remember what he’d been saying at all. There, hanging in her car by a delicate ribbon, was the mask with its drying leaves and flower petals, its twin slumbering runes with their spent magic. He didn’t know whether he should stare at it or look away. She kept the mask, too. She kept the mask, too.


That meant—did it mean anything? Maybe she just thought it was pretty. Maybe she just took it off in her car and hung it there without thinking about it again. Maybe she had been meaning to throw it out, but it had been forgotten in the chaos of the pall. Maybe it meant nothing at all.


Maggie pulled out of the small parking lot in front of her apartment and eased onto the road toward town. “You were saying I am Dean Clearwater’s best what?”


Arthur tried to remember what it had been that he was going to say, but there was a roaring in his ears that he couldn’t quiet, and something like hope burning in his chest.


Beside him, Maggie was focused on the road, each streetlight they passed illuminating her face.


Finally, he said, “His best alchemist babysitter, at the very least.”


She scrunched up her nose and sneaked a glance at him, laughing lightly. “Not a job I ever asked for, that’s for sure. I should’ve let you walk home.”


“Intentional ghoul endangerment?” He tsked and added dryly, “That’s got to be some sort of HR violation.”


This time, her laugh was louder. “Are you going to report me to Edna?”


“I’ll think about it. You’ll just have to find out tomorrow.”


Before long, they were back in front of Bean There, Done That, now dark. “Will you text me when you get home?” he asked.


“Only if you do.”


“Wouldn’t want either one of us to get fired,” he added. Gods below, all he really wanted to do was lean across the center console and kiss her.


“It would be a shame,” she said quietly. After a moment, she shook her head, and then said, “Good night, Taliesin.”

facts.fact: 胆怯抉择：多次开口又咽下，决定 Rory 的烂计划好过看她失望——不想做弄断珠串的人。
半月窗长椅：她膝上摊书旁摞一小堆；书架成拱多为 Diadhan 传说史诗；窗外 Ilex Hall 灯塔/Wilds 饿着。
她的低谷自白：grad school 烧空、不再信任自己；因祖母的 Diadhan 言情译本爱上这门语言。
她的研究起点：第 15 节一行被译错十几遍的诗——她怀疑是习语；文献连读中长出课题。
他的平行人生：Simon 出生那年起的夏天飞来 Galloway 做研究——那时结识两位院长；周末带 Simon 来书店。
facts.anchor: The year after Simon was born

facts.fact: 社死：随手抓的书是《职场难谈》；耳朵烧到发根；他说是给继母买的，她 Sure 递台阶。
公寓阳台：阳台一角水晶承光饰+风铃、彩盆植物在阴郁里发蔫；她执意开紫色 coupe 送他回 Bean There。
